title: Pretentious
author: Unknown
preview: On December 15th, Mudit Chand Narayan, 28, left my house with one nasty smirk on his lips, that still makes it hard to accept for me that he isn’t with us anymore. On the way home, his car crashed into a constructional v...

blocks.content: On December 15th, Mudit Chand Narayan, 28, left my house with one nasty smirk on his lips, that still makes it hard to accept for me that he isn’t with us anymore. On the way home, his car crashed into a constructional vehicle, maybe due to the fog, which crushed the front of the car he was driving. As the eyewitness of the accident told the police, he died the moment his car hit the vehicle. Witnesses told the Police that the car was almost at 100km/h, which has sparked the theories of this being a suicide, but that isn’t what we are here to know.

He enjoyed the first 15 years of his life being an unequivocally brilliant, bright and centre of attraction kind of individual (or at least that’s what he used to tell me), and then I saw him struggling to be above average the rest of his life, which makes me doubt if he actually was even half of what the picture he drew me the first day we talked. And for the rest of our time together, he didn’t dishearten me once for being a predictable one. Even in the way he died.

Mudit loved to listen to music. A very particular kind of music which was lyric heavy and questioned love and the subsequential pain were his go-to these days, but when his music activity crossed 60 hours of listening in the past few weeks, we knew it was getting too much. Police reports say that when the crashed car was found, the song “Main Zindagi Ka Saath Nibhaata Chala Gaya” was playing in it, which further supported the suicide theory. But that again can be pure chance that apart from the mainstream garbage pop he used to listen to, his taste in music was rather sad. He used to say his kids will cringe if they read what he has written, because he romanticizes death a lot, so just for the sake of not getting judged by his own kids he won’t have kids at all. One of his favourite lyric was
“Is it romantic how all my elegies eulogize me?”
-Taylor Swift, 2020
Who knows if maybe he took it too seriously?

A man with very limited vocabulary, all the notes and creative writing pieces he has left behind are filled with cliché analogies and overtly non-poetic and rather dull wording with some words marked with asterisk and * have to google a better synonym for these written in the footnotes which, when found, further added to the disappointment to the ones who thought he was a good writer. One of his notes, as his friends recall, elucidate further on it where he writes how in his first few college years people used to call him “pretentious”, and he didn’t care about it for all those years because apparently, he didn’t know what pretentious meant and couldn’t bother googling it.

He always said that he preferred dying in his 60s rather than as a 27-year-old, because for him death was a pain and the least a human being could do was to not to pass the pain to the ones they cared about, and a 27-year-old has way more people to care about than a saggy 60-year-old. He highly despised the idea of “The 27 club”, or how all the poets he admired from the romantic era died rather young. P. B. Shelley, at 29. Lord Byron at 36. John Keats, 25. No matter how he worshipped these people and their art, he always thought it was a very “pretentious” way to make a fucked-up life sound more poetic, and it doesn’t change the fact that Shelley eloped with a 16-year-old when he was 21, had a 19-year-old wife at home with a kid aged 3, or how Fanny Brawne, a woman with a rather aquiline nose didn’t suck the sap out of dying Keats. But dying 2 weeks before his 28th birthday it still stays questionable if he meant what he used to say.

A week before his sudden demise, in a friendly meet which of which I didn’t have a thought would be our last with him, he blurted out a slightly different version of his cliché line about death. He said, “Death is a pain that deserves to be felt. If you’re going to leave the ones you love in pain, you better go off with a part of that pain.”, which seemed more like his pretentious self at the moment he said it but now feels as if he had it all worked out in his wicked brain.
Buried within his 10,000 Google Keep notes, when I searched for the keyword “Epitaph” out of my anger mixed with the curiosity about the clues I missed or ignored, I found this one.

“You will die one day. Surely, not now, but one day, right? What do you think your final words should be? Do you want it to be another Taylor Swift lyric and to be remembered as a crazy fanboy for the rest of your life…wait there would be no life. You’re planning about something that’s after you have died asshole. Yeah so, no Taylor Swift lyric. You know what, you’ve never seen Gone with The Wind. I hope you do by the time you have died, because believe me or not “Frankly my dear, I don’t give a damn” sounds like a cool mic drop. And even if you haven’t watched it by then, it would kind of convince the people reading your epitaph that you must have been a big-time-moviegoer. You’ve faked your whole life, one more show of that skill won’t hurt anyone will it?”
– Mudit Chand Narayan, circa his 24th birthday
I hope he didn’t die without watching it, because I don’t want him to die a liar, or worse, to be remembered as one. May the dead soul rest in peace.
PS: I can almost bet that if he had to write an obituary of himself, he must have had to Google first what an obituary actually means.

title: The obituary of Death’s intern
author: Unknown
preview: In the early 2000s, one night- the sky, a coal-coloured membrane, with thunder so loud, it felt like two great hands were ripping the sky apart. The downpour was corrosively cold while the creaks of doors could melt ston...

blocks.content: In the early 2000s, one night- the sky, a coal-coloured membrane, with thunder so loud, it felt like two great hands were ripping the sky apart. The downpour was corrosively cold while the creaks of doors could melt stones.
Crow:

I’ve often been told that my work isn’t exactly dignified. It’s the butt of dark humor, it’s widely feared, it’s kind of product you will have to buy from us, one day or another, it moves poets in their youth and the non-poets in their non-youth.

So, who exactly told me that my work isn’t dignified? The only other being that’s in the business. I’m 19 now and two years ago, I was renamed Crow, had the best chunk of my memory wiped out and was appointed as an intern to Death. I said the name was too dramatic and asked if I could call him “Unicorn baby”. He looked me straight in the face and I joked about it being a ‘deathly stare’ and all I got was a shut-your-talking-organ look. Death has always been very dramatic and prefers to call me “apprentice”. My hands and neck have blackened over time. When I asked Death about it, he says that’s it because the hands and the neck are sensitive areas, made for making art, passing judgements on people’s lives darkens them. I was going to ask more questions about sensitive areas but he cut me short. He is very professional about his work and we never have days off; although I get a month every year to myself to go out and be a human. This was the time I met a girl named Sakura.
Now that I have only so much time to live, I might as well get working. I pull out some sheets of paper from the drawer and start writing.

I am now a dead person. Another one bites the dust (great song by the way). I am no more. I have deceased. I am bereft of life. I have wrung down the curtain and gone to join the choir invisible. I have expired. I have left to meet my maker. That being said, let’s talk business. I never got to do things like talk about my personality but I guess this is what I will do before my employer takes my life.

I never really liked pretty things. I took refuge in my sardonic humor. I never understood why humans took death so seriously and I always thought of myself as a pragmatic individual. I had the decent job of keeping an account of Death’s clients and I had to save a copy of their life’s memories onto a pen drive. I had pitch black and numb hands and neck. We travelled effortlessly across the globe and often jumped out of windows after lingering shamelessly near deathbeds, it gave Death a kick to do that and I thought it was neat. I can’t remember much of my earlier life but I bet I’d be one of these humans if I wasn’t his intern. It was all going good till I met her.

She used to idly draw triangles in the sand and told you that something was stuck in your teeth without making it embarrassing. She often sat down while she heard someone talking and always looked people in the eyes. She loved to sing and it was infectious. She used to get frustrated easily and used to mumble a lot. She never gave up on hard things and I wish I could do that. She had ears that stuck out. I’d notice tiny details about her and she made me question my sultry attitude toward emotion. Her hand brushed my neck once and that patch wasn’t numb or black anymore.

I never really got to spend enough time with her. The day Death and I turned invisible and lingered near her deathbed, my heart skipped a beat. I remember how I threw her pen drive and stomped on it so hard that it broke. I ran but it was of no use, Death whipped his robes and dragged me down by my feet; there’s no running away from Death, quite literally. He told me I had two hours before I was to die and that he would not tolerate someone who couldn’t be neutral to something as death.

To meet her was a plaything of circumstance. I know that she is dead by now but whether or not she was with me ceased to be of importance. I could reach out my hand and could touch her. Love and death weren’t opposites but merely things that made humans yearn for life. I can’t remember what my folks were like but I want to put it down on paper that I have felt love and I will have felt death. If she were alive, I think I’d let her know about what I thought of her. Maybe I will have been born twice, as Ian Fleming said, once from the womb and once when I look at Death in the eye.

I hope this obituary finds it’s place in this universe, in the form of ashes or in the hands of someone who can’t read or as toilet paper for a dog. Whatever it is, maybe one thing I can affirm is that like death, I accept this, I am human after all. Uh, how do I end this? Thank you? Man, I really wish I died old school style with the whole piano falling on you in slow motion.
That day, Death returned to this grieving youth. Death was greeted in that two-bedroom apartment with a smirk and in invitation to share a Jack Daniels. Death was livid.

He fixed his stare upon him and the boy found himself sucked into a never-ending abyss lined with millions of stars, each representing the duration of a life, some exploding, some flaring up and some turning into black holes. Against the jet-black vacuum of space, stars indulged in a cosmic dance, disintegrating, consuming and burning. Death reduced him to a self-constricting star, on the verge of implosion, his life dwindling and the boy, made peace with his fate till be was reduced to nothing but a nebula of gas, then to a wisp of smoke and eventually, nothing.

Death stood motionless in the bedroom. He quietly bent over the body and used a pen drive to suck up Crow’s memories. He then, straightened his three-piece suit and grumbled about the inefficiencies of human apprentices.

title: The Unravelling of Lovecraft
author: Unknown
preview: The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of the unknown. H. P Lovecraft Describing Lovecraftian horror exactly may not be possible. In fact, I feel that calli...

blocks.content: The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of the unknown. H. P Lovecraft

Describing Lovecraftian horror exactly may not be possible. In fact, I feel that calling it horror isn’t correct. Dread would be a better-suited word because such literary work doesn’t scare you as you consume it but instead sticks with you, grows, branches until you start to question your surroundings. In a sense, it is very meta because what you go through is highly similar to what the protagonist in a typical Lovecraftian tale goes through. (Except we don’t go insane. Probably. ) The hero feels an intense sense of intrigue as he unravels a massive conspiracy or mystery until he realises that what he has witnessed is beyond his comprehension, driving them insane. Although a unique idea back in the 1920s, this has become a common trope in modern cinema and television.
Weird Tales and the Cthulhu mythos

Lovecraft created a fictional world that almost seamlessly mirrored the real one except for supernatural occurrences. Replete with names of streets,universities, and cities, Lovecraft made the reader feel like they were actually looking at a small-town in the local geography. No other author had managed to create quite as personal an experience for readers.

The landscape’s reality is superseded only by the intrigue attached to the great Eldritch gods, who are a race of monstrous god-like creatures that have existed since the very creation of time and space. Dagon and The Call of Cthulhu are two stories that specifically mention the name of some of these creatures and give us tangible descriptions of their behaviour.

They have a mollusc-like appearance and a slimy fish reminiscent picture of these creatures is painted. They are magisterial beings, and information associated with them is undefined, vague and largely obscure. Here the abstruseness of the monsters ties them intimately with the notion of terror. This ambiguous storytelling allows the reader’s imagination to fill in the blanks and unearths the most profound and terrifying fragments of memory to create a fantastically distorted picture unique to each reader.

The kind of horror they create as omnipotent masters of irrelevant human puppets is disturbing and challenging to put in words. Imagine a worm stumbling upon a circuit board, ignoring it and carrying on with its life. One dull day the worm realises the significance of what it had seen. It is driven mad when it obsesses over what it has seen as a human; That circuit board represents just how meaningless the worm’s life is. Those markings, complex mechanisms and those buzz-like enchantments signify the presence of a higher form of energy. Now imagine that it is given a tiny glimpse into the knowledge that a human possesses. For that brief moment, it feels emotions, and has access to unending amounts of philosophical knowledge. As the worm let’s go, it realises the scope of what it has witnessed. It knows that the microscopic brain it possesses can’t comprehend what it has seen. However, it has more questions than answers. It yearns for another second of vision through this godly lens, and in its yearning and curiosity for answers, it is driven insane. The worm knows that its world doesn’t matter anymore, and anything it can ever do will be inconsequential.

These monstrosities, since then, have gone on to become cultural icons. Their connection to the early stages of the planet, eldritch wisdom, and the sense of trepidation that they radiate have inspired other authors to pick up on them and use them in their own stories. One must credit Lovecraft’s generosity as a writer here as he encouraged and mentored other writers and gave them the license to treat the universe he had built as a sandbox for their visions. It may be because he considered this free advertisement for his work, but it was remarkably progressive for a man as closed-minded as Lovecraft. This widespread fanfiction was the birth of the Cthulhu Mythos.
A journey into the mind of Lovecraft
Before proceeding with the article, it is worth examining just how the writer’s brain developed such a distorted sense of horror.

To say that Lovecraft was a man with issues would be a remarkable understatement. Lovecraft was born in Rhode Island in 1890 and spent most of his tragic childhood in New England. He was born into a wealthy household with elitist ideals; however, his world turned upside down. Over the course of his childhood, his family lost affluence, and his parents suffered traumatic psychotic episodes.

In 1893, his father was admitted into Butler hospital due to a mental breakdown suspected of being a symptom of Syphilis. However, Lovecraft remained ignorant of it and maintained that the reason was his father being overworked and that this state continued until his father’s death. Their fiscal condition was significantly affected after this incident and his mother’s condition deteriorated as well. From historical accounts, it seems that his mother became highly protective of him. Her behaviour resembled paranoia; she did not even let Lovecraft out of sight because of all the ‘danger’ outside. Lovecraft recalls that his mother was “permanently stricken with grief” after his father’s hospitalisation.

However, the death of his grandmother seems to have the most significant influence on his development as a writer. This period was when he started having nightmares about horrifying monsters and eldritch gods.

Lovecraft was an atheist who had started questioning his protestant teachings at a very young age. Upon being told that Santa Claus was a myth, he responded, “God isn’t equally a myth?”. Lovecraft suffered from depression and suicidal tendencies in his adolescent years. He states in a letter that the only reason he didn’t commit suicide was because of his interest in science. Astronomy and chemistry were of great interest to Lovecraft. Even though Lovecraft was highly well-read, he was never able to complete his education formally. He had episodes of severe mental illness, and he could not even go to school for long periods. (It is theorised that the root of these mental breakdowns was the realisation that he may never be able to become an astronomer because he was weak in mathematics. This is suspected to be why mathematics was used as an element of horror). Even on his good days, Howard felt extreme social anxiety and agoraphobia (a fear of places and situations that might cause panic, helplessness or embarrassment). It is worth noting that in his earlier years, he was a shut-in, under the constant pampering of his paranoid mother, isolated and a victim of frequent psychological abuse. These traits were of great significance in his development into a mastermind of weird fiction and the racist ideology in his writing.

Howard’s deranged mental state and pampered childhood left him with lots of fear and conservatism to such a substantial degree that he ended up developing a wide array of phobias. He was afraid of medicine and doctors. He was scared of rain. He was terror-struck by geometry (been there). He was terrified of romance. He was even frightened by colours that the human eye could not see (basically most of the electromagnetic spectrum). He was petrified at the sight of immigrants. Well, I have now run out of synonyms for ‘scared’, so to simply put things, it would be more convenient to say that he was horrified of everything and everyone (excluding the Nordic-Aryan origin New England folk, of course).

As an adult, Lovecraft decided to revive some of the scientific journals he wrote in high school and started creating racist poems praising the Aryan originated white people and declaring African American folk a segway between man and beast. Soon after being done with these catastrophic poems, he started writing for pulp fiction and weird fiction magazines. This period was where Lovecraft had found supporters who would encourage him to write and publish. As awkward as Lovecraft was, he eventually married a Russian Jewish immigrant named Sonia Greene after confessing to her that she was the only woman he had kissed. Their marriage shouldn’t have worked on paper because of his anti-Semitic and anti-immigrant beliefs, but it was surprisingly wholesome.

Lovecraft was never able to support the household because writing fantastical fiction did not pay a lot. Add on to this Howard’s fear of rejection and criticism, which meant that he was very reluctant to adjust to the needs and demands of publishers. Lovecraft still believed in living life like an aristocrat and refused to be seen as someone who works to support himself rather than for his satisfaction. This meant that he lived life on the bare minimum for most of his adulthood and was even malnourished. Lovecraft was never able to gain prominence and mainstream fame, even though his weekly writings in weird tales were pretty popular. This was because he was a prolific writer but not a voluminous one. His writing style was far too archaic and difficult to understand. Soon his mother was hospitalised too, and it is theorised that this was either because of the stress due to the lack of money or because she had contracted Syphilis from her husband. Lovecraft visited her regularly, but she soon died. His wife Sonia did her best to support him in New York with the jobs she could find. Eventually, she moved to Cleveland for a job which meant that she barely saw Lovecraft anymore; still, she kept sending him his weekly allowance. The great depression did not make things easy for the couple either.

They were separated for years on end and eventually decided to take an amicable divorce. Sonia remarried without ever knowing that Lovecraft had never signed the divorce papers, contrary to his assurances. Lovecraft died in 1937 obscure and penniless, but he managed to immortalise himself through his literature.
Inspirations and influence on the zeitgeist

If you have watched television shows like Stranger Things, True Detective or read Stephen King novels, then you already have an introduction to the Lovecraftian brand of horror. Cosmic and existential horror have become familiar tropes in modern pop culture. Their influence is not just restricted to Hollywood; it is also prevalent in Korean cinema, the anime industry and the gaming industry. Junji Ito’s Uzumaki and the game Bloodborne are examples of the masterful adaptation of the Lovecraftian ethos resulting in a delightfully chilling concoction of intrigue, amazement and horror.

Several directors like Guillermo Del Toro, Ridley Scott and Joss Whedon have also been known to incorporate Lovecraftian tropes in their cinema frequently. Even today, his literature is of keen interest to academics and is rigorously dissected by researchers to teach about speculative realism, object-oriented philosophy and 20th-century posthumanism. Although niche, his influence on music is pretty noteworthy too. If you, like me, are an avid listener of heavy metal and psychedelic rock, then you too must have noticed his influence here. Metallica recorded an instrumental titled the “Call of Ktulu” and “The Thing that should not be”, which are full of references to the dark prince of Providence (a nickname given to Lovecraft by Stephen King).
It is obvious that Lovecraft’s prominence in modern culture is here to stay.
It is worth exploring the literary roots of his creation, as it is very telling of the connection between the 18th and 19th centuries and the zeitgeist.

Lovecraft’s grandfather ensured that Howard was a regular reader as a child. Ultimately young Philip developed a keen interest in gothic horror literature. Young Lovecraft had a voracious appetite for reading, and he immersed himself in the library near his home.

Edgar Allan Poe is undoubtedly one of the most prominent and well-known influences to Lovecraft. His influence is evident in Lovecraft’s prose and his gothic settings, such as The Rats in the Walls, Cool Air, and Lovecraft’s interest in burial, ghouls, and death. Lovecraft describes Poe as the “God of Fiction” and has even directly quoted him on more than one occasion. Algernon Blackwood’s The Willows is easily one of the most remarkable cosmic horror tales ever conceived. Heavily featuring themes of mystery, isolation, imprisonment, and a world beyond comprehension, the novella is most certainly haunting. The King in Yellow by Robert W Chambers is one of the most critical works which helps one appreciate Lovecraft to a greater extent. Lord Dunsany, William Hope Hodgeson, Ambrose Pierce, Algernon Blackwood and Arthur Machen are some of the other prominent authors who have influenced Lovecraft.
Bigotry in Lovecraftian literature

Part of Lovecraft’s genius is his ability to make the reader, just for a few minutes, afraid of everything around them. This sense of omnipresent fear and alienation is what codified the genre of cosmic horror. During the 1920s, racism was far more acceptable and commonplace than today, but Lovecraft was incredibly racist even for that time. As much as his close-minded xenophobic, racist ideals disgust me, Lovecraft’s prejudices did indeed influence his fiction. Racism is an essential aspect of Lovecraftian horror, as it was his fear of the unknown which he used to conjure and portray his view of the world.

In the so-called “modern” first world countries, stories of white genocide, super predators, and the master race are still prevalent theories (In fact, they are even leveraged during elections to generate votes out of fearful “nationalists”). The contemporary relevance of Lovecraft will extend beyond what most of his devoted followers would care to admit. Despite his widely known literary techniques and accomplishments, his bigotry and race-inflected narratives can’t be swept under the rug. His disturbing ideals are still breathing, even the most toxic and rotten amongst them.

Lovecraft never even made an effort to conceal his hatred and disdain for minorities; he would openly publish the most preposterous and twisted ramblings on those he considered a threat to his “Aryan” purity. He warned his friends and acquaintances of the Jew’s secret agenda to take down the Aryans of New York and even sympathised with Hitler’s cause. However, his contempt for blacks was even more profound.(Google the name of his cat !) He was a firm believer in segregation, maintaining that any interaction between blacks and whites would lead to catastrophe and destruction.

Lovecraft even tended to get furious upon seeing immigrants on public transport. His wife recalls that his face would turn angry and livid upon seeing workers of minority races. Therefore, it is of no surprise to me that such a racist imagination possesses this uncanny ability to concoct the most vicious and devilish representations of minorities, non-natives, social hierarchies, and political forces to give those depictions vitality and plausibility.

A decade ago, this led to a major controversy. The World Fantasy Award is a prestigious literary achievement given to writers excelling in the field of fantastical fiction. The trophy is a caricatured bust of H.P Lovecraft himself which was meant to acknowledge his masterful precedent in this field. It wasn’t apparent to most how ignorant it was to give the bust of Lovecraft to a black or Jewish author until Nnedi Okorafor (the first black winner of the award) took to the stage to express the internal conflict she felt upon receiving the award.
An eventual improvement? Kind of Sorta?

As much as I have criticised Lovecraft’s bigotry, I want to conclude this article by highlighting his endeavours to change his ways. What follows is not an apologist’s excuse or justification for his actions but a description of how Lovecraft’s philosophy evolved over time.

There is strong evidence that the source of Lovecraft’s paranoia and twisted fears was his isolated approach to life up until adulthood. There was never a time when Lovecraft was not racist; however, his attitude and opinions changed for the better in his last decade.

Of his horror fiction, the work that probably seems the most overtly racist is “The Horror at Red Hook”, which features phrases like “The devil-worshipping Yazidis” and “unclassified Asian dregs”. It should also be noted that it is a treatise on the negative social consequences of the mistreatment of immigrants. The protagonist is also an immigrant. “The Shadow Over Innsmouth” highlights the author’s fear of miscegenation (he was freaked out when he found out that one of his great-grandparents was Welsh). Still, it is a Lovecraftian critique of colonialism. A South Seas trader makes a career out of taking advantage of technologically inferior indigenous folk, until he encounters a technologically superior civilisation and is similarly taken advantage of. The novella “At the Mountains of Madness” ends with the narrator concluding that even monstrous prehistoric beings that look nothing at all like humans but have shared values like scientific curiosity and a love of art should be respected as peers.

These efforts were undoubtedly unsuccessful; “noble savage”, “inscrutable Oriental”, and “magical Indian chief” are still quite antipathetic characterisations even if they were intended to be sanguine.

Ultimately, he did start taking steps in the right direction, even if they were baby steps. This change was possible because he actually made an effort to expand his horizons by socialising with an open-minded approach. He was even accepting of an extremely primitive melting pot philosophy towards American society and ended up marrying a Russian immigrant Jew. That’s not all, though; he even ended up supporting socialism, but that was primarily because of his own poverty.

After having read all about his grotesque ideology, this put a bittersweet smile on my face. It reminded me about a decade-old memory of Modern Family, where the episode concludes with a commentary on whether an adult can change over the course of their life. One of the show’s characters, attempting to answer the question, says that people are who they are, give or take 15% and that too if they really really want to.
People change for themselves or maybe because of the people they love. But sometimes, even that little change is enough to have a positive impact on those around them.

During my research for this article, I developed a lot of resentment for H.P Lovecraft, however, seeing a transformation in a traditionalist as rigid and chauvinistic as Lovecraft gives me hope for the future, considering the scenario of partisan and sectarian contemporary politics.

title: After Thought
author: Unknown
preview: Time. It’s always fascinated me. Something that’s continuous, but also immovable. It’s one thing we can always rely on. Whether we eat or sleep, have fun or work hard, celebrate or grieve, all of it consumes time. You ca...

blocks.content: Time.
It’s always fascinated me.

Something that’s continuous, but also immovable. It’s one thing we can always rely on. Whether we eat or sleep, have fun or work hard, celebrate or grieve, all of it consumes time. You can do anything you want in this world, but every single action you take is governed by the laws of time.

And that time is limited. That’s the solitary reason for the significance of anything we do. If we had unlimited time, we could and eventually would do every activity in the universe. The fact that we can’t do it all, that we only have a limited number of moves left to make before we’re done, is what gives any of those moves purpose.
But I digress. I’m trying to distract myself from what is probably the most important choice I will ever make.

As I step inside the room, I’m blinded by the immediate brightness. From top to bottom, the room is completely and utterly white, aside from one wooden desk in the exact center, with two wooden chairs on either side. On the chair farther from me sits a Latin woman, maybe in her mid-thirties, wearing a white lab coat over a white shirt. I see her name, Sara, scribbled hastily on the lab coat with a marker. I carefully make my way over to the empty chair and sit down. Two buttons sit on the desk in front of me. A simple green ‘YES’ and a red ‘NO’. Large, physical buttons, as if having an actual physical presence lends more importance to the choice.
She says to me, “It’s time for you to make a final decision now.”

I know that I should focus on what I’m going to decide, but I just can’t help wondering how it’s come to this for me. I should be at home right now, sipping a glass of wine on my pristine leather couch while watching some junk on TV.

But if I’m really being honest, I never really did anything like that, even in the good days. Wall Street never sleeps, and nor do it’s brokers, so my life was constantly clouded by never-ending stress. When it all fell apart for me, as it often does for many like me, I couldn’t help but feel just a little bit of relief. Perhaps I wouldn’t have felt that relief had I known what the next three years had in store for me.

The thing is, there’s really nowhere for a broker to go after Wall Street. Once you’ve been kicked out, you can’t force your way back. And no one would prefer a washed up 34 year old guy as their consultant to a shiny new 22 year old, just out of college and with just enough brash confidence to win everyone over. Odd jobs, managing at coffee shops, pharmaceutical trials, I’ve tried everything I could to make money. And while it’s enough for me to survive, it’s just not enough for me to live.

Well, everything could change now. It all started this morning, when two men came to my single-room flat. I was surprised to hear the doorbell ring in the first place, because it’s been a long time since I’ve had any visitors. They were wearing identical three-piece suits, and they looked just official enough to let me know that they weren’t here for a mere meet and greet.
“Sir, we’d like to talk to you for a few minutes. Can we sit down?”

As they got comfortable on my lone couch, well, at least as comfortable as you can get on the dusty old couch that came with the flat, I noisily dragged my plastic chair in front of the couch so as to face them.
They got straight to the point.
“Sir, me and my colleague here are part of a governmental agency, we’d prefer not to say which, and we have a request to make of you.”
I let out a small sigh of relief under my breath. I was almost convinced that these men had come to apprehend me for some of the less than ethical things I did in my Wall Street days.

The other man spoke, “We’re conducting a trial, a research experiment of sorts, and we’ve been looking for potential candidates. And we’d like to inform you that you, sir, are one of those candidates.”
I was confused.
“What, uh, what kind of trial?”
“Something our R&D department came up with, a drug that can alter the function of the brain.”
They must’ve found me using my records from the pharma trials.
“Alter it to do what?”
The other man spoke. “Sir, we’ll be honest with you, we don’t really know how it works, but we do know what it does. They claim that it’ll give you access to all of your memories.”
“Uh, I pretty much have access to all of them already.”
“Oh, I’m sorry if you misunderstood me sir. I meant all of your memories. Past and future.”
“Wait, what?”

“I can understand your confusion. The way they explained it to us is that the brain knows everything about us. There is a portion of the brain that predicts what we’re going to do, our actions in the next couple of minutes or throughout the day. According to them, the function of that part of the brain is restricted. They’ve figured out a way to completely unlock that part of the brain, which will theoretically predict your movements and actions for the rest of your life.”
I just stare at him, speechless for a few seconds, not knowing how to react.
“Is this a joke?”

The other man looks slightly infuriated now. “Look, sir, are you willing to participate in this trial or not? We do have other places to go to.” I don’t really have any friends, at least not anyone who would go to these lengths for a practical joke.
“So, uh, what would I have to do?”

“If you say yes, we’d come back in the afternoon to pick you up and take you to the facility where the trial is being conducted. After you take the pill, the people over at R&D will keep you for some time to observe whether or not it worked. Then we’d let you go back to your regular life, but we would observe you over the next year to see the pill’s effects on your behaviour and health.”
“The next year ? Wait, wait, how much would I get paid for this?”
“Ten thousand dollars immediately after you take the pill. Forty thousand after that in installments over the next year.”
Holy shit. “Fifty thousand dollars!?”
“Yes, sir.”
I realised why they had chosen me. Someone who’s lonely, strapped for cash, but also someone who had enough intellect not to go crazy after taking the pill. Well, at least immediately after.
“So, sir, are you in or out? It’s completely up to you.”
It was a huge decision, too huge for me to make my mind up on the spot. But one simple fact allowed me to make a quick judgement. I hated this life. I’d do anything to escape it.
“Okay. I’ll do it.”
“Good. We’ll come to pick you up at 3 o’clock sharp. Thank you, sir.”

And with that, they both got up and left. A couple of minutes later, I realised I hadn’t asked them for any ID whatsoever, and that there was no way any part of what they said was possible. After half an hour, I’d dismissed the whole incident as an absurd prank. But sure enough, exactly at 3:00 PM, I heard my doorbell ring again.
Curious, I rapidly opened the door to find one of the men who had talked to me this morning standing in front of me.
“What happened to the other guy?”
“He didn’t think it was necessary for him to be here for this.”
I recalled that the man who hadn’t come this time was the more irritated one.
I was taken to a black SUV and notioned by the man to get in the back. As I sat down, he suddenly gripped my hand firmly and swiftly injected the contents of a syringe into my forearm.
Startled, I shouted, “Hey! What the hell is this!”
“Sorry sir, I can’t let you figure out the location of the facility we’re going to.”
Even as he finished his sentence, I started feeling drowsy. Within thirty seconds, I was completely knocked out.
I woke up to somebody shaking me lightly.
“Sir? Sir? Good, you’re up. Let’s go.”

He held my arm as I was groggily led through many hallways in an old, empty building. We eventually stopped in front of a door with a piece of paper stuck to it. On the sheet the words ‘CANDIDATE 14’ were printed.
“Good luck, sir.” He opened the door and notioned at me to go in.
And so I find myself here, with an impossible choice.
The woman in front of me is saying something.
“Hey, Ryan? Ryan?”
“Sorry, uh, Sara, I think I just zoned out for a minute there.”

“It’s okay. So, I think you’ve already been briefed about what we’re trying to do here. But we have to make sure you’re fully committed to this. If you want, you can say no, walk out of here, and pretend like none of this ever happened. If you say yes, there’s no going back, so choose carefully.”
“I assume that you’re-”
“One of the scientists involved in this project, yes. I’m here to answer any and all questions you might have.”
“Okay. So what happens if I walk out of here and try to contact the media about all this?”
She laughs a little and says perfectly calmly, “Rest assured we’ll ensure that doesn’t happen.”
I didn’t feel like inquiring further about the meaning of her ominous words.
“So I was thinking about the science behind it, the unlocking the potential of the brain thing, and I just-”

“Wait, wait, wait, that’s what they told you we’re doing? God, they never listen properly. That’s a very crude and shallow way of describing what we’re doing here. It’s like comparing, uh, knowing the way from here to your house to all of Google Maps. Anyway, just leave the science to me. Have you been notified about all of the effects of the pill?”
“They said I’ll see my future?”
“Well, yeah, that’s basically it in a nutshell. You will have all of your memories from your future.”
“But how is that possible? Isn’t the future uncertain?”

“No, it isn’t. Is your past uncertain? Certain events will take place in your life. The problem is just knowing what those events will be. We don’t fully understand the brain yet, and maybe one day we can figure out how it knows your future accurately. But for now, all we can tell you is that it’s guaranteed you’ll remember it all.”
“And it won’t melt my brain or anything?”

She laughs again, in the same slightly condescending manner as the last time, before replying, ”We’re way past that phase of testing. This is mostly just to see the psychological effects of the pill.”
“Has anyone ever taken the pill before?”
“People? No. Well, my coworkers are in the other rooms with other candidates, so maybe one of them has taken it by now. But you’re part of the first batch.”
“What do you think I should do? Should I take it?”, I ask, even though I know what she’s going to say.
“Look, I know you think I’m here to convince you to take it.”
Touché.

“But that’s counterintuitive to this project. If you’re not mentally ready for the pill’s effects and you take it, it’ll ruin our observations. If you’re sure you’re ready, then and only then should you take the pill.”
No one speaks for a minute.
“Philosophically speaking, this is a hot mess. There’s no objective way for me to decide whether or not to do this.”
“But an objective opinion doesn’t matter. You’re the one who’s here. You’re the one who’ll decide.”

“Well, even for me, there’s no easy solution. On first thought, I’ll be getting fifty thousand dollars, so of course I should say yes. Thinking a little more about it, I realise I’d be giving up my whole life to this, that I’d become a guinea pig for some experiment, so I should say no. But then again, at this point I don’t really have much of a life to give up in the first place.”
She takes a couple of seconds before she speaks.
“I take issue with your definition of giving up your life.”
“Why? I’d know what’s going to happen for the rest of my life, wouldn’t I?”

“Yes, but that doesn’t mean that you wouldn’t experience any of it. Just because you know what’s going to happen doesn’t mean that you won’t actually do it. When you rewatch a funny movie, you know you’ll still laugh at the funny parts, right?”

“Yeah, but-” “Even though you’ll know the pains and joys that the future holds for you, you’ll still experience them fully. The only difference is the foresight of what’s about to come. And honestly, most people would love having that foresight.”
“What do you mean?”

“Haven’t you ever had days where you didn’t take the time to appreciate when something good was happening for you? Where you were miserable for some unrelated reason and later regretted not being as happy as you could’ve been that day?”

“So you’re saying that because I’ll know when the joyous moments in my life would be, I could live those to the fullest.” “Exactly. And not only that, getting past the rough times would be easier too if you knew for certain that things would get better. The anxiety of your future during your bad times would vanish.”
“That’s a double-edged sword though.” “How so?”
“The lack of uncertainty would create a lack of excitement. I’d know exactly what’s in store for me for the years to come.”
“Again, that isn’t purely a negative thing. You lost everything at your job at Wall Street, right? Imagine how much better you would’ve handled that if you’d have known it was coming.”
“Maybe I would’ve handled it better, but all the joy I had during those years at my job would’ve been lost if I knew I was going to lose it eventually.”
“Are you saying that knowing something is temporary makes it harder to love?”
Wow. Unbeknownst to her, Sara had just beaten me with my own views about life and time.
“Okay, I admit you’ve been able to refute all my arguments.”
“I’m not arguing with you, Ryan. I believe in the work we’re doing here a hundred percent, and I wouldn’t be asking you to do this if I didn’t.”
“What exactly is the work that’s done here?”
“Well, we’re in R&D, so R&D. Research and development.”
“Experimental science, right?”
She nods.
“Then isn’t all of this just a way to try and control nature? To manipulate the things that come naturally to us, that make us fundamentally human?”
“Well, wait a second now-”

“Life isn’t meant to be lived with permanent certainty. We’re not supposed to live life to the fullest, we’re just supposed to live life. You said I wouldn’t have any regrets, right? But I’m supposed to. We learn from the mistakes we make. If I know everything about myself, I’ll have nothing else to achieve for the rest of my life.”

“Just because you have a knowledge of what will happen in your life doesn’t necessarily dictate that you don’t learn from it further. The full emotional consequences of the things you’re going to do will only manifest themselves after they actually happen. When you watch a football match that you’re sure your team will lose, you still feel bad after they lose even though you knew it would happen, right?”

“But that’s not entirely because I watch them lose. It’s also a matter of losing hope. Hope that maybe a miracle would happen, that something out of the ordinary occurs. If I do this, I would never have that hope anymore.”
I pause for a second.
“I just realised that taking this pill would mean I wouldn’t have any hope for the rest of my life. With all my actions defined, I can’t possibly believe anything will change.”

“Okay, this is going to sound harsh, but do you really have any hope right now? I’ve been through your file. You’re aggressively unemployed, you’re borrowing money left and right that we both know you’re never going to give back unless you do this, and you look like a shadow of the person you were 5 years ago. We’re giving you financial security, I think that’s hope enough.”
Even though none of what she said was new information to me, her blunt words broke me a little. I tried to hide my pain to preserve whatever dignity I had left.
“First of all, ouch. Secondly, I can scrape my way through. Who knows, I might win the lottery, or I could open a consultancy, or maybe even run a chain of successful yogurt shops. Who knows?”
“You could, if you take the pill.”
“That’ll ruin the feeling of achievement. It’ll feel like cheating, like it wasn’t me who figured out a path to success, but someone else who I’m now copying.”
“But won’t you feel that much more relieved knowing that your future is secure? If you think that you’ll lose all hope, you’ll also technically lose all fear.”
I consider this for a moment.
“But it comes back to the same thing. If I have no hope, if I have no fear, I don’t really have a reason to live.”
Sara’s finally beginning to look a little agitated now.

“I feel like I’m banging my head against a wall here. Knowledge and experience are two separate things, and one of them cannot make up for the absence of another. Just because you figured out how to tie a tie once by looking at a YouTube tutorial, doesn’t mean you know how to do it forever. And even if you learn all the steps to tying one, you’ll never really know until you can until you actually do it.”
“Wait, are you telling me you don’t know how to wear a tie?”

“Look, this discussion is endless. I can keep coming up with arguments and relevant metaphors and you can keep refuting them with your philosophy bullshit. I think it’s high time you decide. Are you in or out?”
I suddenly realise that this argument is really just another way for me to stall, to postpone the decision a bit longer. Enough. Now it’s time to take a call.

If I wasn’t as miserable and desperate as I am now, I wouldn’t have even considered taking the pill. But I hate my life. Fifty thousand dollars will do me a lot of good. I could clean myself up, shift somewhere better, maybe even meet someone. Even if I know what lies in store for me, so what? Whatever it is, it’ll definitely be better than the end point of my current trajectory. And maybe I’ll have a new sense of purpose. I’ll finally be part of something that’s not only about me.
“Okay. I’ll do it.”

I press the yes button in front of me. It flashes with green light, then a small door opens on the side of the button. I stick a couple of fingers inside and grab the one and only, almighty pill. It looks exactly like your run of the mill pharmacy shop medicine, a tiny red and white capsule containing god knows what inside it. I can’t really wrap my mind around the fact that all the stress and tension of today revolves around this one miniscule tablet.

“Great. Now all you’ve got to do now is swallow it”, Sara says. “In a minute or two, you’ll start to feel a little bit drowsy and then there’ll be a sudden prick in the back of your head. After that, you should be able to remember everything.”

I place the pill in my palm and slowly bring it up to my mouth. I can feel my hand getting clammy and my forehead starting to sweat. It feels more like a fifty-pound rock in my hand than a dainty little pill. As I get closer to swallowing it, I feel a sudden rush of adrenaline. Immediately, something clicks inside my head and just as I’m about to swallow it, I stop.
Sara looks confused.
“What’s the problem?”
I put my shaking hand down on the table and rest the pill there.
“I – I can’t do it.”
“Oh you’ve got to be kidding me”, she says as she looks at me, now visibly frustrated.
“I’m sorry”, I say as I walk out of the room, feeling a twinge of regret but also one of relief.
As I walk out the room, I see the man who had taken me here, standing guard next to the door.
“Sir? You chose not to take the pill in the end?”

“I couldn’t. Right as I was about to take it, my heart was beating, I was full of adrenaline, and I had no idea what was going to happen next. I can’t live my life without that feeling. Maybe someone else can. But not me.”
While the man led me out of the compound, I had time to think about what I had just done. I was anxious, regretful, unsure of myself and of my future- and I was loving every second of it.

author: Unknown
