blocks.content: ~Mudit Chand Narayan

The sound of the cold, steady stream of water was acting like a lullaby to her ears. It’s been twenty minutes of her sitting on the wooden bridge that somehow was the only passage from one side to another in the miles of the river’s flow.

She had her eyelids closed, and her ears were doing nothing but listening to the noises the water running underneath her was making as it was pummeling on the impenetrable rocks underlying the riverbed. Her legs were hanging into the river from the bridge-side. The occasional drizzles of icy-cold water were making her quiver as they touched her toes.
She was a photographer.

Had she looked up, the glorious mountains glistening in the north would have been her dream come true. She spent her childhood snaring the flowers of her garden in her camera, and her early twenties capturing her dreams; but today she was sitting stock-still.
She unconsciously broke what seemed an eternal stare, and palpated to her right where her camera was. Fumbling through the jacket and things lying there, her hand fell on the camera.

She groped it. Adjusting herself on the ridge of the wooden bridge, she delicately picked it up. With her eyes closed, she felt the button she once clicked to capture a million memories in that little frame.

She touched the lens, oh those lenses. How much she cared about them. The whole set she had, how she was proud of each of them. She knew their functions by heart, and she never shied off from bragging about her knowledge about cameras.
She rolled her fingers on the ridges of the lens, zooming in and out, and then left it in her lap.

“Riya!” She heard her name echoing the valley from a distance, which meant that it was her time to leave the tranquility of this valley, which was the only thing she enjoyed. She grasped on her shoes, and then her jacket.
But as she was picking up her jacket, she heard that particular “knock” too.

It was the lens. The other lens she had left on her jacket when he took her there on the bridge and left. It rolled, and rolled, and as she knew it was falling, she kept throwing her hands in different directions but could not get a hold of it.
It tossed to the edge and then it fell.

It took a last bump on her toe, and then it was gone. Gone in the roaring waves of the waterway rippling under her feet. An accident, an imperceptible recklessness, and she lost the lense she loved the most.
Just the way she lost her eyes three months ago in that accident.
The cold water had made her feet numb, more numb than her soul at the moment. And as the sound of waves crashing on lifeless stones went louder, a sob built up and went unnoticed.

The chilling wind was enough to freeze someone’s guts as she wore the jacket. “ Coming “, She replied to the voice that called her what seemed like a millennium ago and she clenched her camera to her chest.

A camera, which once was the other face of hope to her was not leaving any chance of reminding her of her frailing dreams and the feebleness of her knees. The lens that fell was continuously paining her with the fact that she couldn’t even see how it fell off the bridge like her fragile hopes tripped when she was hit by the car that day.
“ Click “, a painfully unnatural sound filled the valley. And though she could not see the pictures, she kept clicking as a tear rolled down her cheeks and disappeared midway.

title: “If you could see your whole life from start to finish, would you change things?”
author: Unknown
preview: It was a freezing winter night; the sky was silky black covered with patches of clouds looking like velvet cushions on an enormous black bedspread. In a cold isolated room of an old broken-down house, a candle was burnin...

blocks.content: It was a freezing winter night; the sky was silky black covered with patches of clouds looking like velvet cushions on an enormous black bedspread. In a cold isolated room of an old broken-down house, a candle was burning with a flickering flame, so dimly that it might disappear any moment. This faintly glowing flame was probably the only thing which kept the emaciated and shriveled creature, too meek to be called a man, alive. The man might have been in his early forty’s but he looked like he might fall into his grave any day. His flesh had been reduced down to a skeleton, his skin looked like a wrinkled wrap cloth for his bone cage and his hair flowed down his tilted head like dried up rivers of sorrow. This man was called Scarus Stephens. He sat curled up in corner of the room near the window staring into the deep open void.

His deep meaningless trance was broken by sudden stroke of heat as if the sun itself had shown up at his door. He turned his head and saw that the candle which was about to die off now held a huge flame, so big that it wasn’t possible for a candle to produce it, but there it was, blazing in-front of him. In that moment an inexplicable thought got stuck in his mind. He raised his hand and almost mechanically plunged his hand into the flame. Instead of burning him the flame consumed him entirely and he vanished from his room as if he was never there to begin with.

Listening to this, Scarus’s mind went blank. Never had he heard or thought of such a thing being true. It was almost impossible for him to comprehend this, but at the same time it seemed all too familiar. He thought this was a trap, some sort of black magic that might bind him in a loop of time, a vicious cycle from which he might never escape. But alongside this, another thought had sprouted in his mind, he thought that could his life be any worse than it already was? In this conflict he tore his scarce hair apart while the flame burnt in his face. Finally, he took a leap of faith. He said, “If what you say is true then I am ready to make every possible endeavor to make this pathetic life of mine into something more decent, something more fruitful and satisfying. But tell me this why have you brought me here, what significance does this time sequence hold.” But the flame gave no reply, it just started to glow yellow again and engulfed Scarus. When he opened his eyes again, he was at the exact same spot, at the exact same time to where and when he was first teleported to. Once more he ran towards the hut and knocked at the door. Once again the woman opened the door, but this time Scarus gave a feeble smile which almost disappeared immediately and he said, “good madam, I was wandering in the forest about 2 miles from here when I came across this piece of land, and I could tell that I would not die, for across the huge green plain I saw this, I saw your hut. Good madam, please help me, I am thirsty from 2 nights and if I speak anymore, I think my throat my dry up and I may die.” The woman took Scarus inside and gave him a mug full of water. As scarus gulped down the water, she prepared a simple meal for him and told him “You can stay with us for a while, until your health permits you to travel again.” “Thank you, I owe my life to you in more ways than you can ever imagine. But tell me this, you said that “you could stay with us” but I can’t see anyone else apart from you. Does anyone else live here too?” The woman sighed, a sad and devastating look shadowed her face and she said, “My son Scarus lives here with me, at least for now. But he wants to move to the big cities he wants to work in a factory. He considers this life of a farmer as something low and disrespectful and thinks that by working in those cities with smoke for a sky, he can gain respect. I have tried everything to stop him but he won’t budge from his decision. His father went on the same mad trip 3 years ago, and he hasn’t returned. Sometimes I fear he is now one with the smoke.”

Scarus realized how apt his mother’s words were. In about 10 years his life would start crumbling apart and he would not be able to stop that. So, to her he said, “Ma’am you have saved my life, let me repay the favor. I think I might be able to reason with your son.” Late in the evening young scarus returned when he saw his older self. “Who is this mother?” The mother said, “This is your uncle Stephen, he works in Manchester in an iron mill. He has come to live with us for a few days.” But young scarus was already lost in his dreams after hearing about Manchester. He rushed to his older self and cried, “Uncle you have to tell me how the big city is, it must be so exciting working in an iron mill away from all this. You have to take me there uncle, I beg of you.”

Older Scarus sighed deeply and said, “You have a tender mind child, you cannot see the hardships the big city brings with it. Here you have fresh water, clean air to breathe, a long farm to run. In the city you will be deprived of all this. At your tender age the smoke of the air will ruin your lungs and the water will burn your stomach. Your legs will grow weak and your body frail. Look at me, do you want to look like this when you grow up, do you want to feel as weak and useless I feal right now. Don’t rush to the big cities for so called notions of a respectful job or life. My life is in no way respectful or self-satisfying.” Hearing this young scarus grew wild and yelled, “You have had your time in the big city but when it comes to me you blabber on with these lectures. Why can’t anyone understand my dream of living in big house, in a famous city, with titles so extravagant that people call my name with respect”. “You think you will achieve that by working in an iron mill? You can’t even comprehend how wrong you are. But I don’t want to kill your dream, instead I will show you the right way to shape it into reality.” Saying this he took out what little money he had with him and gave it to young scarus, knowing thirty years earlier even that trivial amount would be like a treasure to him. Seeing this the mother came forward to interrupt but old scarus said, “please don’t refuse this ma’am, you won’t believe me but I really want to repay my debt to you and want to see young scarus as someone respectful and not someone as disgraceful as myself. I give him this money not to travel but I urge him to spend it on something more productive, something that will develop his skills in fields which the big cities lack. The big cities are filled with machine men with mechanical lives but the intellectual capacity of the people is so weak and low that it is almost shameful. But imagine among all those mechanical men there would be a young scholar, someone with a strong intellectual aptitude and command over knowledge so vast that people would look up to him. By the time you achieve that amount of knowledge and come to the cities you would have grown much older and the environmental factors wont effect you with the same severity as they would now.” The last few lines triggered a sort of mania in young scarus. To him if what his so-called uncle had said was true was a golden route to his dream. He cried, “Is it true. Can a scholar command respect of that stature? Is it true that a scholar would be more respected than an iron mill owner? If that is the case you have done me great favor. I will surely try your way of realizing my dreams. If nothing else it might comfort my mother a bit that I would stay back with her for a few more years.” Scarus gave a gentle nod of approval and looked at his mother who was oblivious to who he actually was, for her consent, not that he needed it that that age but it was an old force of habit to seek her approval. The mother too was convinced because it gave her a chance to hold on to her young beloved son a little longer and not lose him right away.

The next day when every one was asleep, scarus snuck out of the house and walked to the spot where he had thrown the candle. It lay there beneath the tree; its flame had died off. Scarus went ahead and picked it up, but the moment he held the candle in his grasp, his surroundings dissolved and he stood on a single piece of rock with red fiery flames swirling around him like a giant vortex. It was as if the sky, the earth and the air itself had started burning and it was all closing in on him. A voiced echoed amidst this chaos, “This is not the end of it scarus, you have only delayed your downfall but it will take much more to save your life from falling apart. Remember every gruesome mistake that you have made. You have to correct the decisions that made your life so distasteful.” With this the flames collapsed onto scarus and he found himself on a street in Manchester. Towards him, a young man was approaching. He wore a borrowed suit, a shabby old overcoat and carried a gigantic trunk by side. It took some time for him to realize that the man was no other than himself, only a few years older than when he had first arrived in the city. It struck scarus at that moment that at that young age he was a mindless, reckless and a spendthrift lad, who had fallen so deep into the vices of the city that they had drained him of all his money. He had surrounded himself with extravagant men, men who were rich and spoiled and hollow from inside, men who had money and time to throw away and men who had pushed him down to that disgraceful life. By the time he shook away the thought, he saw that his younger self had already walked past him, and was going to enter a pub, only he didn’t know that it was one. Old scarus rushed and entered the pub behind his younger self. He saw that young scarus was sitting alone on a table, when a group of men were approaching him. He rushed and took a seat with his younger self before the other men could. Young scarus hadn’t recognized him from the time when he had visited him on the farm, so he asked, “who are you old man, can’t you see that this table is occupied.”

“I am sorry if I have startled you scarus. I think you don’t remember me and then again why should you. You have only met me once a few years ago and only for a couple of hours. So let me introduce myself again. I am Stephen your uncle”. He saw that young scarus had now started to remember and in few moments, he even exclaimed, Why then its you, uncle Stephen. I can’t believe I didn’t recognize you after what you did for me. I think I have gone down the path you had told me to. I wanted to revert back to my way of doing things but mother always convinced me to the contrary. I have come here only after she said I could go, I realized if I had left her then it would have been devastating, both for her and me. But now we have sold away a part of our land. We have enough money for my travels and education and for her to live happily.”

“I am so proud of you scarus, that you have achieved something that most men don’t even dream about. I should apologize for leaving you like that back then but I had my reasons which I think you will understand in due time. But this isn’t the end scarus. It’s a long walk ahead and trust me when I say this there are not one but innumerable ways of ruining everything you have achieved till now, and nobody shapes them but you. I know I am in no place to tell this to you when I live in such petty states, have wasted my life and haven’t even cared to ask about you in such a long time, but still think of this as an advice and not the blabbering lectures of an old man. Think about them if you feel fit to do so. You have grown into a fine adult and can think for yourself, but I wish someone had told me all this when I was your age, so I am just doing my part so you don’t feel the same way.”

Scarus smiled awkwardly, and why wouldn’t he when a relative who he hadn’t seen in years, had met him in this manner and had started to give him life lessons. He was about to say something when old scarus interrupted and said,” I know all this might sound very strange to you but let’s do one thing, I will walk out of this pub and the group of men drinking at the far end of the room will come up to you and offer you a drink, now it’s up to you what answer you ill give to them. I am not stopping you from drinking, I am just asking you to mind the people you surround yourself with.” Saying this scarus stood up and walked out. After about half an hour, young scarus came out, half drunk and giggling. Scarus approached him and said, “Enjoyed ourselves did we?” young scarus looked and screamed, “Hey uncle Stephan , you are still here? I thought you might have disappeared again. I was not hoping to see you for next couple of years.” Old scarus gave a half earnest smile and said, “Let’s get you home”. Young scarus gave him the address of his new house and he took him there, literally carrying him from time to time. He put young scarus in the bed, undid his shoes and put a blanket over him. The room wasn’t much and didn’t have any thing else to lie on so scarus himself slept on the cold floor. The next morning, he woke up and found his younger self still fast asleep. He shook him till he woke. After young scarus freshened up, he sat down and said,” Uncle Stephen, I had the best time yesterday. That group of men you talked about; they had some really fascinating ideas about living one’s life. They told me a lot of things like, I should dress up in more fancy clothing, should go out with them for drinking more often and the best of all, they told me of a thing called gambling, it sounded so exciting.” “As I had expected.’ Said old scarus. “Try to remember what I told you before leaving. You create your own ways to ruin your life. Tell me once more what your dream was. As far as I can remember it had something to do with commanding respect and achieving a status in the society didn’t it? Tell me this by dressing up in fancy clothing and spend your money on drinking, gambling and living a superfluous life, how would this help in achieving your dream. It might make you look good for a year or two in the eyes of pretentious people but after that you would fall in your own eyes, realizing what a pretentious fool you had been, if just you had not taken that one wrong step, If only you had not forgotten what you really came here for, if only you had not given into worldly temptation but instead had paid little heed to these vices and stuck to your dream you wouldn’t have spoiled away your life like this. Its not too late now, you have just looked into the wrong lane, away from the main path, you haven’t stepped into it. If you tilt your head back to where it was, and keep on walking straight, not turning into ruinous paths, you will achieve something much larger than your dream.” A little of this wise knowledge did get stuck into young scarus’s head. His older self knew that not because of anything young scarus had said as a reply but by the warmth of the burning candle which had reappeared in his trousers. This meant that his job in that time sequence was finished. He took his leave from young scarus. As he walked down the street, he wondered what the flames of time had in store for him next.

“Nothing else my friend, just that your hand did phase through the servants and they actually can’t see you. Infect only I can see you. The reason is I am you but now you don’t exist. The old and emaciated scarus doesn’t exist anymore, because neither did he work in a mill to begin with nor did he succumb to worldly vices. He became the man of his dreams, the one u couldn’t become, and the one you became all the same because I am you and the young scarus was also you. So, the person who ruined his life was you, the person who helped you improve yourself was also you, and the person who is standing Infront of you is also you. But you don’t exist anymore because your terrible past doesn’t exist anymore. You don’t have the candle with you because when you changed the past you didn’t find the candle to begin with and hence it remains here with me in this room.” saying this the scarus in the fine clothing pulled out the candle from a drawer in the table. He held one end of it and asked scarus to hold the other. At the moment when both their hands touched the candle, the old emaciated scarus turned into the green flame and sunk into the body of the new scarus. Moments after this transfusion, the new scarus, who had fainted, came to his senses. He was filled with strength and energy which he had never felt in his old emaciated form. He had a sense of pride and dignity about him which he had always dreamt of. On the table top stood the candle, burning with a small fading green flame. Scarus shed a single drop of tear and blew the flames away, uttering a final thank you. He realized that the voice in the flame was his own, pulling him upwards from the deep abyss of chaos he had fallen into.

title: Red and Blue
author: Unknown
preview: I remember when life was more complicated. When people were allowed to be nuanced, and could have multiple, overlapping identities. When people could depend upon their family for unconditional love, whether they were Red...

blocks.content: I remember when life was more complicated. When people were allowed to be nuanced, and could have multiple, overlapping identities. When people could depend upon their family for unconditional love, whether they were Red or Blue. Back when you could leave your house, and wander aimlessly without half the people you met eyeing you with suspicion. Then the Reds won the elections, and changed the laws to keep themselves perpetually in power. Or did they just use the same Emergency laws that their predecessors, the Blues, had had used to quash dissidents? Ever since then power has changed hands like clockwork, between the two in a series of revolutions and counter revolutions. No one even remembers anymore. It doesn’t even matter anymore. I’ve heard from old-timers about how in their day, people would discriminate on the basis of stupid things like religion. Nothing like that exists anymore. One’s affiliation, Red or Blue, is marked in childhood, and then nothing else matters. Familial bonds are washed away as the concerned Party takes charge of the child’s “education”. Children go to either Red schools or Blue schools. But their days are spent in the same way, reciting the names and birthdates of prominent leaders of their respective factions. They attend weekly self-criticism sessions, where they repent for their actions over the past week which may have been even slightly sympathetic to the other side. All rational thought has crumbled under the duress of unrelenting dogma. I come from a complicated place. It is a Red-majority area in a time when the Blues are in government. Talk of liberation and justice is common, even though these words are nothing but hollow shells now. Red leaders are frequently rounded up and promptly shipped off to prisons on the most frivolous of charges. Even the Blues live in fear of getting their throats slit by their milkmen or maids. If a Red on the street saw a Blue get injured in some horrific accident, they wouldn’t dare help him. Not when they could be seen by their fellow Reds. All of this vitriol was a result of the distrust of their own, as much their terror of the unknown. I used to work for a newspaper, you know. I was a Sub-Editor in the Objectivity Department. My job was to make sure that all the reports coming in were as close as possible to the truth. “Man, 35, Murdered by Neighbour” would be changed to “Red Brutally Murders Innocent Blue”. I think you can figure out for yourself which side my paper leaned toward. Often, it would extend to changing the details of a certain event. Although it wasn’t as if we had much of a choice. Reporters and editors alike who seemed to sympathise with the Reds had a mysterious habit of disappearing mysteriously. It could be something as minor as printing about delays in construction of a Blue project. So we did what was needed, and slowly what we wrote became the truth. This is the story of how I got swept in the tide of hate, yet managed to find my peace. The day it all started was an ordinary one, or as ordinary as it could be in that atmosphere of noxious hatred. I was at the Office, just after lunch break, during which I had eaten biryani from a nearby shop. Now, let me tell you about that particular shop. The owner was an old man, one who had seen governments and parties come and go; and all he cared about was keeping his business open and his family fed. When the centre was Blue, he would hang banners on his storefront which declared his loyalties. And when the tide turned, he knew how to adapt. He had two of every license and identification required to run a business. It was like that for a lot of people. After all, it didn’t really matter who you supported, as long as you did it loudly. Anyway, on that particular day, I sat in the Office, awash with soft amber 4 o’ clock sunlight. It was almost time for our daily pledge of allegiance to the Blues. That was when, all of a sudden the shouting started. I ducked just in time as a brick flew in from the window right next to me. I looked out from the first floor window to see absolute pandemonium on the streets. A huge crowd advanced from one end of the road, smashing through everything it passed. Shops were afire, as big men with lathis roamed about smashing windows and beating people. And the looters! They were everywhere, scurrying about like rats, gathering everything that they could. The man on the adjacent desk, Singh, was shouting hysterically, “What is going on?! Why are they doing this?”. This was no time to lose composure. Everyone knew what this was about. Later that evening, Das, a rising young Red leader, was about to deliver a speech at the festival grounds. Before sunrise, reports had started coming in of a big raid by the authorities at Das’ residence. They had found a lot of incriminating evidence, and apprehended him for “treasonous activities”. What those pieces of evidence and activities were, no one seemed to care. I can only imagine the madness that must have been unleashed as the Red protests turned violent, and met with Blue counter-protesters. During the commotion inside the Office, I turned a furtive glance outwards and noticed a mob forming at the entrance to the building. Quickly, I ripped off my Blue armband, and threw down my citizen ID as I rushed towards the back exit. A young clerk, who I did not recognise, must have noticed what was going on and had the good sense to follow me outside. And he did so just in time, for as we hurriedly headed out into the street, we could hear the crashes and the shouts as the mob broke into the Office. I had only one thing on my mind: survival. Once outside, I saw the charred remains of a torched biryani shop. The next few hours were chaos. I couldn’t go back home, the Reds in the neighbourhood must have obliterated it by then. The only real choice I had was to somehow escape into the countryside. Once the Military Police took hold of the city, there was no telling whose side they would take. Of course, being loyal to the Blue government made it seem obvious, but there was no telling if that government would be able to survive this. Things like this happened often, and hold on power was elusive, and fleeting for both sides. I turned to Ali, the young clerk who had been my companion upto now. Suddenly we were engulfed in a crowd. There were men with crowbars, hockey sticks, and basically anything that could be used to inflict injury. They were shouting things that made no sense, as such zealots were wont to do. I could make out “Justice for Das!” and the like; these must have been Reds. I noticed Ali still had his blue armband on. This was going to be ugly. I did what I had to. It was terrible. They were all around us, and there was a moment of expectant calm. It was not as if they were hesitating to kill us; it felt like a call to action for me. A quick punch to the face, and Ali was down on the ground. “You filthy Blue bastard!”. The words were coming out from my mouth, but I didn’t feel like I was the one doing this to Ali. In the next few moments, the mob descended on him as I tried to get lost in the crowd. I was nearing the city gates now, just a short distance from safety. That was when I saw it. I don’t even know who they were, Red or Blue, but they were trying to kill a child. A child. I remembered the torched shop. What they had done to Ali. What I had done to Ali. And I realised that the only way to make up for what I, and we as a society did upto now was to reverse this descent into madness. One act of fraternity at a time. No more boundaries, just love for the fellow man. Even though the city gates were in sight, there was no doubt in my mind. I was going to save that child’s life, even if it meant my death. I jumped into the throng.

title: The Call of the Void
author: Unknown
preview: ~Vijay Bharadwaj Orange leaked from the clerestory. Ankush nudged me. “What’s the time?” “Almost six.” “Man, wish we had some powers and stuff to get them out of this line, this hunger is uncontrollable now.” “Yeah, I gu...

blocks.content: ~Vijay Bharadwaj
Orange leaked from the clerestory. Ankush nudged me.
“What’s the time?”
“Almost six.”
“Man, wish we had some powers and stuff to get them out of this line, this hunger is uncontrollable now.”
“Yeah, I guess”

We’re not in some surreal dimension, Anks. Grow up. It was good food for the imagination, though, but we needed none of it right now. The queue at the Cultural Programme Registration Desk was dawdling. You couldn’t have seen the line moving if you weren’t in it for at least half-an-hour, like we were. The weight of the Les Paul on my shoulders was proving to be less tolerable minute by minute. Finally our turn came. We all smiled. The senior at the desk looked at us three.
“What’s the band called?”
“The Void”
Tushar came up with that name. He thought the moniker went well with our grungy, dark style of music. He was right – the name did feel apt.
“How long will your performance be?”
“5 minutes?”
“Yeah, 5 minutes.”
“Do you have a title for your performance that our anchors can use?”
Wait, we didn’t give it a thought. Suddenly, the two swagger looking dudes on either side looked a bit dazed. We started prodding each other and whispering – “Say something?!”
The desk interrupted the chaotic murmuring.
“Guys, if you haven’t decided a name for your performance yet, take some time and convey it to the anchor before your gig on the stage, fair?”
We yeah’d our way out of there after writing down our names and phone numbers on the list.

The sky had turned into a more serious orange. We were on our ways back home. Ankush started humming ‘Back It Up’ to the beats of our footsteps, which became faintly perceptible when Big T started patting his thighs to mimic the claps. It was the first song we’d written together as a power trio. Anks did the drums, Tushar did the bass and I did the axe (and we still do). I did most of the singing as well. We loved that song – it had banged at all the audiences we had performed it in front of and we were certainly going to start our performance this Friday with it.

“Hey you two, let’s meet tomorrow morning at 11. Practice ‘At Hell’s Door’. The chords are gonna need some serious preparation. We’ll do it again together when we meet.” We wrote ‘At Hell’s Door’ and ‘You Can Do It’ during the Summer Camp a couple of years back. We were going to perform these two as well in our 5-minute feat for the Cultural Programme of the School Fest ‘Angaara’. Writing songs like this would eventually become our refuge from the usual mundane. It was one essential dynamic that fueled this friendship.

I was near the Town Clinic when I saw this squirrel, bang in the middle of the road, absolutely still. It was probably enjoying getting baked in the sun or something – how do I know? I was looking at it the whole time – wondering what it’d do next. Suddenly, I see this grey Alto making a sharp turn from a decent distance. Any animal with a little aptitude would have easily shown a bit of reflex action and got out of the way. This cute little idiot however, decided to jump intentionally right into the bumper of the car when it came speeding closer. All I saw next was the car going past me. Why would it do that? I shoved away the thought quickly though, since it seemed equally idiotic to be thinking about each and every of those thousands of animals that become victim to such incidents.
“Rest in power, Mr. Acorns.”

Ways separated at the township ring road crossing and I reached home. Profuse sweating and a busy day at the rehearsal had dampened me literally and mentally, and I needed a towel, so I asked Sneha for it. A towel arrived flying from where the living room bends into the kitchen. While I was drying myself, something rustled under me. It was a letter, which had developed creases for obvious reasons. Next thing, my interest was piqued.

It was addressed to me. In the history of our living at this house, never ever had we received a letter addressed to me. We’d seen many improbable things – snakes in our bath, chasing monkeys inside our living room, Grandma threading a needle in the very first go, but this one was new. Maybe it was a conspiracy ploy by all the crores of Gods that exist in my faith, to keep me from creating a nuisance for Mom, Dad, Sneha or for that matter, anyone around me. They perceived me as this highly volatile and ambitious figure that can get upset or anxious or excited about ANYTHING. That’s what they say, at least. I respectfully disagree, however. Indian families do exaggerate things.
Coming back to the letter, it said on the cover:
“Mr. Vijay Bharadwaj,
F-21, Nand Gram,
Gandhi Road, Delhi-18”

and that wasn’t it. The handwriting. It almost looked typed. It was so perfect – it wouldn’t had given itself away if it wasn’t for the ink that got diffused at a few spots. Perfect Didot-style typography and ligatures. “Jeez, that’s some talent right there.”

Was it some famous artist that noticed our music and wanted to call us in to work with them? Nah, that would’ve been a stretch too far. We weren’t even the best band in our own school. Wait, I did turn all my work in before the deadline, didn’t I? Yeah I did. Besides, Miss Gautam wasn’t going to take the hardship of writing an actual letter, especially when I did attend her classes sincerely. Neither was it a handwriting that I recognized from before. My brain was on the verge of going bonkers.

But there were no stamps. No idea why. I hadn’t even opened the envelope yet, and it was raising an alarming number of question marks in my head. Sneha asked me to stop shrieking. I have always had suspicions about her not being right in the head.
So, I took out the sheet of paper inside the envelope and I remember gawking at it consistently for the next fifteen minutes. It said:
Welcome. Use it wisely.
Regards,

I thought the sender’s name would appear magically or something. I held it up against the lamp, tried shaking the paper, even put it in water, as the movies do it. Nothing appeared. And besides, welcome WHERE and use WHAT wisely?! This was probably a joke by one of my classmates. God bless their sense of humour, if they have any. There was no use for soaking wet junk like this. My aims for the dustbin have never been better.

I dozed off and woke up for dinner. At the dinner table, everything was pretty usual. The food was not the most exciting thing so I was engaged in thought about every other random thing that was in the room. Amongst the usual clatter of the cutlery, my fluttering eyes got distracted by a desperate Sneha trying to reach that last piece of pickle at the bottom of the jar. She kept poking a spoon at the bottom of the jar with increasing impetus and decreasing patience. As soon as my eyes focused at her, something brought a prompt change to her facial expression – as if some inexplicable power had captured the reins of her reason; it was a sudden change from a mildly displeased poker face to one of extreme frustration. Did some unknown force possess her? What possibly could’ve happened? The next thing that happens – there is a nasty shatter. Sneha threw the jar onto the floor in a fit of bitter vexation
and it got smashed into a thousand pieces, scattered all across the wooden tiling in the room. Fortunately, no shards of glass aimed itself towards the table, so there were no injuries.
“Are you mad or what? Why did you throw it?”
“Ugh, guess who has to go to the market again.”
“Sorry sorry sorry sorry, I don’t know how, I just… sorry.”

I remained silent. There was something wrong with how the course of things went today. The squirrel and then Sneha. It was not typical of what I would see every day. Was the letter also related to what happened today? The mental exhaustion caused by this mystery was too much to handle.
Not a good night’s sleep. I had already slept half of my evening with that siesta and all I was doing now was staring at the ceiling and thinking what on God’s lovely Earth was that all about.

There was certainly some third party involved. It couldn’t have just been a coincidence. Even if it was, my sense won’t accept its existence. And what was the letter about? Who wrote it? Why were there no stamps? What was the text about? Imagine a cartoon of a person and squiggle a big fat ‘Ugh’ on the head. That was me.

Was it really a possession of a power? Wait, did the power itself write the letter? That could’ve been a reason as to why there was no sender’s name. But what did it want from me? It seemed too surreal to be true.

But had there been incidents in other parts of the city, there must have been a report. Out of all us mortals, why did it only happen to me? For a good hour while I was thinking what did power would look like – nasty blood-lathered creature with horns or a ghost with a handlebar and a vintage monocle? Also, if I assume it only happened to me, do I happen to possess that power? I mean, things only happened when I looked at them. The squirrel was well and conscious and then it suddenly stops as soon as I see it? Sneha was on her own trying to get the pickle out and as soon as my eyes focused at her, she throws that jar away out of nowhere? People…do things…when I see them?
“Wish I could summon…”

A howling wind started blowing outside as soon as I thought of summoning the mysterious being. Eerie scenes. Suddenly, I was gasping for breath. I couldn’t see anything. Darkness, not even the faint moonlight that peeked through the curtains. Something held onto my throat tightly. I cried for help but even I couldn’t hear it. For a moment, there was peaceful oblivion and suddenly, it seemed like I was let go. There was light. My senses worked. I guess I knew now what the story was.

I had the power to enforce people’s intrusive thoughts upon looking at them. Inducing the Call Of The Void, as Google says. Some unnamed power had endowed this ability to me, out of nowhere and it expected me to use it wisely. Wait, didn’t I imagine having a power while I was in queue for the
registration? I had this power all that time? Well, shove it. I guess I am going to have some fun tomorrow.

I woke up in a jolly good mood. I felt like a superhero, with newborn abilities. My eyes were my weapons and my shields. And I felt pretty good about it. It was showtime for some much needed mayhem in this ordered world. The road joining my residence to the school was my arena. Starting from my house, the first victim was my pet Labrador Jimmy. My mom was watering the plants in the lawn right in front of Jimmy’s eyes. As soon as it got close to mom, I shifted my focus on Jimmy and it jumped straight into the wet soil under the watering can, to have a shower. The poor boy must have resisted the urge so badly! Jimmy got dirty in the cool mud and certainly enjoyed it, unlike my mom who was looking at her squished marigolds that she had grown with weeks of patience and care, with immense disappointment.
“Stupid creature.”
On my way, there were a lot of wild roadside flowers. They didn’t budge a bit when I directed my sight at them, so I guess plants don’t have intrusive thoughts. It would have been cool if they did.

The very next minute, a boy in his early teens came cycling from the turn ahead of me. It was time to put my powers to test again. A car followed from behind speeding past me. As soon as the car came parallel to the cycle, the powers captured control of the boy and induced the boy’s urge to speed his cycle into the car. Good thing, I looked away immediately, so all the boy experienced was a little wobble.
Phew, that was a close call. With great power, indeed comes great responsibility. Not too sure if I would care about it that much, though.
The road was didn’t have much bustle, so I couldn’t have any more lab rats to test on. I was assured, however, that I would get a lot of them when I reach school.

It was preparation time for everyone at school for the Programme so not a lot of studying was happening. I saw a corridor on the second floor with a lot of juniors involved in decorating the artboards. I walked through the pathway giving a generous amount of eye to every being. The peaceful passage transformed into a warzone of utter chaos when I trodded upon the scene. There were glue bottles and paintbrushes being hurled down the second floor. I am pretty sure a few would have jumped down, had I not closed my eyes immediately. One little chap tried to hang himself to a nail in the wall with both his hands like a house calendar and fell down, becoming a subject of immense laughter for those around him. One could film this in slow-motion and create a serious hero entry cutscene, no kidding. The intensity of things happening was incomprehensible. The most enjoyable part of all this was how quickly the victims of this power’s summons change their mind about doing what they had the urge to do, when I take my eyes off of them. It was instantaneous and highly comical to look at.
I went to an empty classroom where I was supposed to meet Ankush and Tushar for the rehearsal. “Hey, did you think of any names for the performance?”
“Oops.”
“Ugh, think of it and tell me soon. The anchors are pestering me for it, saying they need it for practicing their script.”
*my phone rings*
“If you sneak in a phone like that into school, remember to put it on silent at least.”, Anks said.
It was a call from Kshitij, my best friend from my old school. Man, 5 years since I last talked to him. Unfortunately the call got disconnected and a voicemail followed, which said,
“Hey Vijay, this is Kshitij from Bal Bharati. See, I am here with a few other of your classmates from your time and we wished if you could meet us here. Come to the tank terrace of the Acad Wing.”
The offer to meet Kshitij and a few of my other old schoolmates couldn’t be turned down. It was a lot of good memories with them, and I couldn’t wait to meet them after such a long time!

It was a 15 minute walk by road but one could reach there through an unpaved road through the township jungle in 10 minutes. So I took the shorter route. It was a dense jungle in those times, and had grown even more so, over these years. After 10 odd minutes of solitary trodding amongst these vines and shrubs and under these mighty canopies, a ray of light peeked the sea of green and there was Bal Bharati in front of me.

It was a desolate sight. It was probably a school holiday – no one to be seen around, not even the guards. The school hadn’t changed one bit in these years. Still the dusty brown paint on the patterned walls, the same rusty gates, the same corridors and even the classroom windows weren’t changed. I paced up the stairs to reach the rooftop where I meet Kshitij, Arhum, Kshuanish and Prashant.
“The five Pandavas are back, what say, my fellas!”
“Man, it’s been so long…”

A string of high-fives followed. It was an anecdotal trip down the memory lane. Everyone had their fair share of stories and incidents to converse about. Arhum even brought the classic salted wafers from the halwai near his residence, as he always used to do when such rooftop powwows were scheduled (no wonder he’s gained a sizable amount of weight in these years).

It was 3 pm. As we were talking to each other, I walked towards the small railing of the terrace to check the view out. The vines that grew, as if they eavesdropped on the melting pot of memories that was being filled here, the whole township that looked very small in scale. Even the famous Wall Of Confession of our terrace where a lot of cheesy rumours about student couples were born, was even more coloured by now. Guess the culture never died.

But as soon as I looked down, a strange power looked to dominate me. It was a very evident déjà vu, from last night. My senses withdrew from my body, there was darkness. My body felt heavier and out of my control. An uncalled-for power hindered my breathing. My shoulder drooped down like a withered Mimosa flower. Something was hammering my insides to make me jump down the railing. It seemed

like a coma. My consciousness got sapped out of my soul slowly. As hard as I tried to fight it by jerking my hands, it was pulling me to the edge as if I had no energy of my own, quite effortlessly. Then, there was nothing.
Next thing I know, Kshitij and others were around me, trying to wake me up. As I regained my senses, I looked around at the blurry world around me. And then,
*Missed Call from The Void*
Call of… the Void?
*1 new message from The Void*
“Back At You.”

Back at me? My body started to shiver at the sight of this message. I felt helpless and limp. Blots of darkness again started appearing in the nooks of my eye. What was happening and what did I do to deserve it? I was breathing heavily, as if a choked throat was let go. I coughed and even threw up. Prashant passed some water for me to drink, but then…
*2 new messages*
“The first words of the three songs that we’re going to perform!”
“The name for our performance!”
The sky was orange. Yet again.

title: Call of the Void
author: Unknown
preview: ~Ishita Vyavahare Anna Anna walked onto the edge of that 20th story building. A few hours ago, Anna’s daughter’s ECG monitor screen showed the straight, green line she’d been taking as an impending but inevitable loss. H...

blocks.content: ~Ishita Vyavahare

items: Anna Anna walked onto the edge of that 20th story building. A few hours ago, Anna’s daughter’s ECG monitor screen showed the straight, green line she’d been taking as an impending but inevitable loss. Her cancer had spread to her abdomen. It felt like it was her fault although Anna knew that any rational person would know better. Words of consolation came in and all she did was gave to them were a few murmured thank-yous and head nods. She craved solitude. Amidst her grief, the sight of anyone who wanted to speak to her ended up nauseating her and although they meant well, she wanted to shut them off. The 20th story building was the one right in front of the hospital building. The building was a beauty, exclusively reserved for big timers and big business offices. It wasn’t uncommon to see people in expensive clothing and limos lingering around and entering this building. Anna went there solely to look at the city from the terrace. As she looked out from the surprisingly low railings, she sighed which came out as a white puff disintegrating into the November cold. There were buildings everywhere, and from where she looked, tiny shops dotted along streets like ants lining up chaotically yet orderly. This side of Manhattan was particularly well lit. As she peered down below, the lights from buildings layered from one floor to the next almost as if she was staring into a never ending, downward, psychedelic tunnel. People looked like specs of dust floating in and out of her vision. Her eyes registered movement as if she was on a hunt; wild instincts taking over. Her heart was racing, her pupils were dilated. All she could feel was the urge to jump and with every breath, this feeling intensified. At this point, every cell in her body yearned to let go of the railings. With quivering hands and a mourning heart, she had flashes of perplexation; what was this feeling? It was as if her rational mind couldn’t explain this and that was terrifying. A hand reached out and grabbed her arm and yanked her back into the terrace. “Ma’am, you better be careful.” Leon was confused. Was this woman suicidal? She looked like she could jump. Leon thought he saw a silhouette lingering around here. This woman clearly needed to get to lower ground. Anna, blinked a couple of times, still in a daze. What had just happened? She could answer this question just as much as a kid could talk about the stock market. But she loved this feeling. It was wild and untamed. Leon was convinced that this woman needed help. Leon escorted her all the way to the elevator and then left her to her own.

Leon Leon knew he had to report to the manager in about twenty minutes. But this woman bothered him. He straightened his clothes and took a deep breath. He was almost done with duty. A dull headache and an aspirin were almost a routine now. He was reluctant of go back to the lobby. He headed straight to the terrace. His post as a security guard was transient. He despised having to live like this. He decided to use his twenty minutes in an introspective solitude. He gravitated to the terrace and he couldn’t tell why. The flurry of night lights and endless arrays of building floors and straight down. There was something deeply assuring about this place. What was a breeze down on the ground was a storm of sorts up here. Yet, one could hear the blood gushing in his ears. This deadly combination of sounds made the terrace a spectacle for Leon. But this place was high. A jump spelt doom. Possibly an unpleasant splutter for the people directly underneath. 20 stories was no joke. What there was; eerily enough, an inexplicable urge to look down below, at your coquettish doom. The doom catcalled him. He looked straight down; he shouldn’t have. He checked how high this place was. Then, he couldn’t stop staring. He felt light-headed, a first in many weeks. He could feel a pulsating exhort to go on and let go. He had the urge to jump. It was real. He didn’t want to die, he wanted to feel alive, weightless, floating. It was this rapt attention that the doom caught. He was aware of this confused feeling. His rationale and his biology clashed. His switched in and of reason like the pendulum of a grandfather clock. He tore away from the void and forced himself to look away. He didn’t want to do anything stupid. He shook his head and briskly walked away from the edge. He pulled his trench coat close to his neck and brushed off the invasive thoughts. What the heck was he doing? He quickly stepped into the lobby where Walter was doing the standard drill. He needed this raise. He’d worked really hard for the last three months. “You’re late.” Walter wasn’t in the best of moods. Was he? Leon checked the time. He was nearly twenty minutes late. Did he really spend forty minutes on the terrace? It felt like five. The next day, Leon pressed his thumb into the biometric device. He couldn’t stop thinking about that spot on the terrace. It appalled common sense but fascinated his instinct. He wondered if that woman was doing the same thing up there. Just as he was thinking this, he saw her outside the lobby window. Talk of the devil.

Anna Anna came back to the hospital to complete documentation and formalities. She waited outside so that filing was complete. Unlike last night, it was comfortably warm and sunny this morning. The overhanging clouds of last night metamorphed into scattered and connected webs of clouds. She was caught by surprise when she saw the same man jogging up to her as the one, she met last evening. “Morning. I didn’t get a chance to thank you last evening. Seems like I walked a little too far upon the edge.” She was embarrassed.

blocks.content: “It no problem ma’am. I just wanted to ask, what were you doing there last night?” Anna was struck by the candidness of the question. “What do you mean?” “I mean, did you uh…feel something up there?”

items: Leon Leon realized that this woman was emaciated. He was a sensitive person; he had to be, after these years of living in poverty. “I don’t know what you are talking about.” He knew she was covering up with words. He knew that she knew. Leon just nodded. “Okay. I’ll just leave you to it then.” He turned around and began to walk to the street. Manhattan was a place where time was a commodity sold in scanty amounts if you were poor; Leon had to get to work. “Wait! I felt something up there.” Leon turned around. The woman looked like she could collapse at any moment. He walked back up. “Yeah. Me too. Did you feel like jumping?” “Yeah.” “I’m Leon Kaspersky.” He extended his hand. “Hi, I’m Anna Alkaitis.” She took it. “I felt like I was going to jump, but I wasn’t suicidal. Does that make sense?” Leon was clearly shaken by this experience. His hand was warmer than hers. She needed to eat.

Anna/Leon Anna nodded, agreeing. At this point, she had to sit down or she’d double over. “Can we go sit somewhere?” Leon nodded. The café they went to was lit with warm yellow lights and smelt like biscuits and coffee. Anna took a bite of her sandwich and sipped at her coffee. The coffee travelled down her throat and she felt the warmth descent into her belly. She sighed and felt relieved. “I think we should investigate that place.” Leon knew he was late. But he felt and inexplicable pull to that place, he wanted more of it. “You mean go up there again?” Anna thought this was an absolutely frivolous idea. She had no plans of risking her life again. But she was curious too. Was it just that place or just a coincidence? “Yeah. You see, I had an experience up there and then, had it again this morning.” “You went up there again? Are you crazy?”

blocks.content: “No, I didn’t. I was at home. It was……controlled.” “What?” “Yeah, I mean, I was staring at my window and it happened again, except it was a sort of alertness.” “You mean you kinda induced it?” “I don’t know.” “What do you mean?” “I don’t know.” Anna was ambivalent about this. She looked into her empty glass which now had coffee residue at the bottom. She looked at the grainy patterns and fiddled with her spoon. A second later, a snake made of lightning slithered around her veins. Like electricity, her eyes hardened over the glass. The glass looked like a never-ending tunnel. Doom called her battle cry. Anna was sucked into the depths. She could feel herself falling into a labyrinth of brown coffee inside. She felt alive and looked away. She saw the surface of Leon’s face. Every irregularity bared itself to her. Like fractals, everything was connected but independent. She saw the order in the apparent randomness. Leon called out her name. “Anna?” She was simply staring into space. “Anna!” He speculated that it’s Doom again. Leon took her by the shoulders and shook her. She snapped out of it and inhaled deeply. “Let’s go up there.”

title: A Small Sky
author: Unknown
preview: She holds it to her lips like life does breath. Her glasses fog over as the steam lingers and rises away from the cup, restless spirits of tea leaves blooming away from their ceramic purgatory. Sweat clings to her brows...

blocks.content: She holds it to her lips like life does breath. Her glasses fog over as the steam lingers and rises away from the cup, restless spirits of tea leaves blooming away from their ceramic purgatory. Sweat clings to her brows and trickles down the ridges of her neck.I ask my mum why she insists on drinking pipping hot tea in the July heat.”It’s the way I’ve always done it. It’s the way I like my tea” The ugly pink walls of my school stare me down, our navy flag drooping without winds to set sail to.I may never see this place again,I think, never smell this place again. My vision doesn’t blur, my throat doesn’t burn but my heart swells and falls.My dad’s in the army so we were always a moving family,3 winters and 4 summers in a place was part of my education but the thought of a lost winter would always feel the coldest, sting the hardest.I would go inside our temporary house one last time and with everything in boxes, it almost looked like the place we once came to, not the one we were leaving behind.An empty house screams back when you scream, sings back when you sing, your time there bounces off the white walls and the rectangular place much paler than its vicinity, one can only imagine, must have been a lovely portrait of its inhabitants. In our case, it was a random picture of sad stags. Since seventh grade, the circumstances had me settling down in Kota for a period of 6 miserably hot years and as a result I had to maintain friendships for periods longer than elephant pregnancies. Now mind you, we still changed houses twice because no house should have to(read can)bare my family for more than two years.But I stayed in the same school and talked to pretty much the same people and remembered birthdays for the first time in my existence.Now,I was never a school enthusiast,6 am is too early for life.The only reason I went was to make teachers uncomfortable with excessive eye contact and to lose debates. Every single one, every single time.As I came out with my last school mark-sheet in hand,I looked at the basketball court with naked hoops, a quiver of yellowing trees shooting early autumn leaves in the blue breeze.I never turned around but through the exit, I could see what led to it,I could see it all.The arching centre of the second floor school library where the flags hung,I felt the air conditioning of our reception caressing my summer sweat and the way it always smelled of new carpets.I saw pigeons fighting for nesting grounds through busted up windows and I saw our class making obscene gestures at the newly installed cctv, huddling too close to spin bottles and throwing pens across five rows of teenagers. I heard the electric bell that sounded like jangling pennies by the kg .It had sounded like freedom for six years and I realized I wanted to hear it once more, that feeling of a lock clicking into place. As the class of 2020,I suppose we had to be the most introspective of recent graduates, what with the exam dates getting pushed out of sight. Our affair with jee wasn’t wanting in eyerolling drama. I spent two years professing my love at ungodly hours and proving my worth but when she’d finally agreed to meet me, she stood me up. Later she’d reason she had just learnt of black market toilet paper and I’d work on forgiving her. It was 4 months of patience wearing thin, stretching like sidewalk bubblegum under the bellowing feet of the virus.Everything that wasn’t happening stacked up in jenga walls around us, threatening a clumsy fall if we were to try and look for window slats. The unprecedented had happened and I was finally ready for the signature dystopia virus to up and wipe out everyone except me, my dog and two suitable love interests. Alas, that wasn’t meant to be either. Change is a frightening thing, but change for us came in the guise of masks and sanitisers and plate banging instead of the usual first year college diploma in procrastination. College didn’t happen when the sticky summer sun melted the sky in blinding white, when the mechanical whir of fans made you lethargic and the vanilla dripped off your chin and onto your favourite shorts or even when the sky serenaded us with gentle droplets, reclaimed the greens and painted every house anew. When lightning split and forked in the sky and distant bombs dotted the horizon, when every rain smelled like hope, if perhaps hope is petrichor and a little bit of animal faeces. College didn’t happen in the humidity when you could’ve drunk water from thin air or even as the trees changed to austere bones piercing where they held the purple hued sky. The ways of lockdown were harsh on some, for me it was the realization that if this feels normal, maybe I should step out more. And ironically I did, me and my brother walked Tuffy, the barking cat all through lockdown and then some. I had the non-paying yet respectable job of gathering dog poop in newspapers that announced celebrity resolutions for 2020 and how Britain still couldn’t decide. I came to like this obligation mostly because I like songs and I listened to the whole discography of Airborne Toxic Event while Tuffy strutted through the manicured apartment lawn and stopped to feel the winds on his whiskers every once in a while. I learnt that if you’re counting feathers on your balcony, you can only ever count the ones coming down because the sky camouflages the ones that soar above concrete and chimney smoke. I launched an experiment on the ways to make Maggie with only water and seasoning.It took endless 2 am tastings to get it right. I went through the same notes over and over again.Monday bled into Tuesday,June into July into August and climbing six flights of stairs in a mask left me waiting to catch a real breath. The city around us had always bustled with students, early morning garbage disposal music, drums at the most unfortunate hours and me singing along to Don’t Cry. It all fell silent one day, there were no roadside sellers clogging arteries with their oil drenched livelihood and over-speeding imbeciles honking away at the smoke in the air.There was silence and then there were dogs. The dogs that, forgive me, went to the dogs with people not risking coming out to feed them ,with people struggling to feed themselves. The dogs howled and yapped from their empty bellies, their bones protruding at the meagre flesh on their bodies, they ate away hungrily at the silence, tearing scrapes off of it with their gleaming teeth, licking and swallowing with their gaping wet mouths. Change is a certain thing. September came around,I sat my exam in three parts nerves and one part nonchalance,I don’t remember much from those six hours but I looked at the timer often. I can hear that silence too, the silence of shuffling eyes from the screen to paper to the timer, it played over like a broken record. The silence of pens screeching in haste and chairs being moved delicately, to nurture this silence. The silence that slithered and coiled, asphyxiated my thoughts after the timer showed that I had, at last, done my time. I expected change to be climactic, not me sitting in a car outside my school with a mask hanging from my neck like a chin rest while I scanned my report card before the deadline at 5. I think we’d all expected to be homesick by now, instead we are home and we are sick of the virus. I’m not inherently excited about college like I thought I would be and I wonder if I’m still waiting for the sky to come down and tell me that something has changed drastically. For the house to tell me that I had lived in it, for this winter breeze to carry with it autumn leaves, for my mother to switch to Redbull. I am sitting amidst great beauty as I write this, surrounded in acres and acres of hills dotted in dirty green pines and telephone towers standing upon them like scarecrows. The sky is small here, my mum said the very first day as the hills obscured the world outside. Tufts of white chrysanthemums are abloom and the roses lipstick red, nature flushing crimson at its own beauty. There are snow-capped mountains to the north and a crow is singing the chorus to Don’t Cry as it passes over my head. Things are changing, it’s winter after all. Things are changing, the mist that shrouded the top of the mountains yesterday has descended to the foothills. Things must be changing,I start college tomorrow. A watched pot never boils but I can’t seem to take my eyes off of it.
